name: Northeast Face
beta: Approached via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail to Dutch Miller Gap, the route climbs about 500 feet of heather and rock steps up the northeast ridge to an open bench, then crosses a snowfield into a cirque below the east face. Two short (roughly 60-foot) belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class rock lead to the summit area; at the top of the first pitch, move climber's left to find the direct finishing pitch. Reported variations include the north ridge from the upper snowfield, or four pitches of roped class-4 slabs taken directly. A separate approach from Pete Lake/Summit Chief camp reaches Little Big Chief's northeast basin and a ridge notch guarded by a low-5th-class crux (a large vertical crack) that most parties rope up for.
overview: The peak's original 1939 first-ascent line and its easiest way up: heather, talus and snowfield travel along the northeast ridge to a cirque below the east face, finished by one or two short belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class (occasionally low 5th) rock to the summit.

current.approach: From the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where the road is gated), follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley about 14-15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, passing Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the Williams Lake trail junction along the way. Little Big Chief sits immediately southwest of the gap, reached from the gap itself by an off-trail scramble up the peak's east slope/northeast ridge, with a short but exposed class 4 notch as the crux below the summit. An alternate, longer approach comes from the east via the Necklace Valley Trail off Foss River Road (Skykomish/US 2 side), crossing La Bohn Gap before dropping to Dutch Miller Gap. A second long approach comes from the southeast: the Waptus River Trail from Salmon La Sac to Waptus Lake (with an unbridged river ford below the lake), a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, then the Dutch Miller Gap trail up past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap. For this specific route: continue the standard Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail all the way up to Dutch Miller Gap, then climb directly above the gap onto the peak's northeast ridge/face — no cross-country detour into Summit Chief Valley needed.
approach_variant_names: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the two short belayed pitches — using tree or sling anchors for any rappels — back into the cirque below the east face. Cross the snowfield and descend the roughly 500 feet of heather and rock steps on the northeast ridge toward Dutch Miller Gap. Parties who approached via Pete Lake/Summit Chief instead downclimb the ridge-notch crux (often roped) and drop into the northeast basin to regain camp. Do not improvise a shortcut gully: a first-hand account of this east-side face descended the East Face at class 3 but became cliffed out about 600 ft above the valley floor after straying into a northeast-trending couloir.
current.detailed_rack: A single rope, helmets, and slings for tree anchors or possible rappels are the standard kit; no dedicated cam/nut rack is typically reported as necessary for the short roped sections, though a few slings for natural protection are worth carrying.
current.pro_needs: Minimal formal protection: the two roped pitches are typically belayed off natural features (trees, horns) rather than placed gear, so slings and cord for anchors suffice. An ice axe is useful while snow lingers in the cirque.
bivy: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it

name: South Couloir
beta: This line was skied as part of a multi-day (May 12-14) south-to-north ski traverse of the Twin Sisters Range by Chris Simmons, Mark Allen, Greg Balco, and Paul Kimbrough. On the second day one of them skied Little Sister's South Couloir, singled out as the trip's best line. The traverse's technical crux - about 40 m of 4th-class rock, 100+ m of 50-degree ice, then 100+ m of rappelling ending in a fixed rappel with a knot pass - came later, on a crossing of the range near South Twin Sister, not on this peak.
overview: A snow and rock gully on Little Sister's south side, reached by climbing to the col southeast of the summit and traversing onto the south aspect. It has been skied during a traverse of the whole Twin Sisters Range and climbed in winter as a moderate snow gully with a bit of mixed ground near the summit.

current.approach: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. The bridge is gone and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
approach_variant_names: Green Creek Glacier to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, then round onto the south side
current.descent: Reverse the line: one winter party made a double-rope rappel from near the top and a second rappel below the col southeast of the summit, where a single 60 m rope reaches. The couloir has also been skied.
current.detailed_rack: Light alpine kit rather than a rock rack. One 60 m rope is enough for the documented rappels: a winter party carried two 60 m ropes, used them together for one rappel from near the top, and found a single rope would have done at the col. Bring a picket or two for snow anchors, a few nuts and slings for rock anchors on the mixed ground near the summit, and plenty of cord or webbing plus rap rings; there are no reliable fixed anchors, so plan to leave gear.
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin and improvised. The south-side gully is snow and rock, climbed unroped in good conditions, with a bit of mixed ground near the summit where the dunite offers occasional horns, blocks and small nut placements; it is coarse and generally solid but is not a splitter-crack medium. Expect to move unroped or run it out on moderate snow and save your gear for anchors. Because you will rappel, budget cord and rings for two stations you may have to build from scratch.

name: East Shoulder
beta: Approach from Summerland alpine meadow via the Fryingpan Glacier, aiming southwest toward Whitman Crest notch at 9,000 feet. Cross the Whitman Glacier and ascend to the summit block, where a short, loose class 3 scramble that includes an exposed notch about 15 ft under the top reaches the true summit. The route is graded as a moderate alpine climb, feasible for competent glacier climbers but not for beginners.
overview: Little Tahoma Peak (11,138 ft) is the third-highest summit in Washington and the most prominent remnant of the much larger, older Mount Rainier edifice that has since eroded away, standing as a jagged andesite pyramid on Rainier's east flank above the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers. First climbed August 29, 1894 by J.B. Flett and Henry Garrison via this same east-shoulder line from Summerland. The rock is shattered, hydrothermally altered andesite, and the peak is chronically unstable — a December 1963 collapse released roughly 14 million cubic yards of debris that ran about 4 miles down the Emmons Glacier and White River valley. The East Shoulder is Mount Rainier National Park's most popular independent (non-Rainier) alpine objective: a moderate glacier climb across the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers finishing with a short, exposed Class 3-4 scramble on famously loose rock.

current.approach: From the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead (3,800 ft) on the Sunrise/White River Road (WA-410), follow the Wonderland Trail south along Fryingpan Creek about 4.5 mi to Summerland (~5,900-5,950 ft), a subalpine meadow with a stock/hiker shelter and toilet. The Fryingpan Creek Trailhead parking area and the spur trail from it close from late September 2026 for the length of the park's Fryingpan Creek Bridge project (construction planned for 2027-2029); while they are closed, park at White River Campground and take the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. Leave the maintained trail there and climb north of Meany Crest across the Meany snowfield, making a rising traverse toward rock outcrops around 7,000-7,350 ft — the standard high camp. From camp, gain the Fryingpan Glacier, rope up, and traverse southwest to 9,100 ft Whitman Notch for the first view of the Whitman Glacier, then cross the upper Whitman Glacier to the peak's high shoulder before the final steep snow couloir and Class 3-4 summit block.
approach_variant_names: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland
From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the summit block (or make a short rappel from the old anchor), descend the east shoulder and re-cross the Whitman Glacier over Whitman Notch (9,100 ft), then the Fryingpan Glacier back to high camp/Summerland. Early in the season the Meany snowfield below camp allows a fast glissade/plunge-step descent; watch for sun-cupped, softened crevasse bridges on both glaciers by afternoon, and avoid lingering below other parties on the loose rock during the descent.
current.detailed_rack: Typical glacier rope-team kit: one rope (~30m class) per 2-3 person team, 2-3 snow pickets, and spare carabiners for crevasse rescue.
current.pro_needs: None on the scramble; glacier protection as conditions dictate.

name: Live Free or Die!™
beta: P1-3 (5.8-5.11) climb bolted overlaps; P4 (5.12, V5 crux) is height-dependent rightward crimping with an optional pendulum; P5 (5.11) is mostly bolted with a delicate V3 mantle finish; P6 (~5.11d) is a thin crack needing small gear; P7 (5.11+) roof climbing into a 5.10 slab traverse; P8 (5.10) a splitter hands crack to M&M Ledge; P9-11 follow Thin Red Line to the summit.
overview: Despite its name and grade label, Live Free or Die! is NOT a boulder problem — it is a full 11-pitch, roughly 1,200-foot free route up Liberty Bell's East Face (grade 5.12- yds; crux may feel 5.12b for shorter climbers), sharing a few meters and belay stances with the Independence Route. Established in summer 2017 by Seth Keena-Levin, Nathan Hadley, and Blake Herrington. Mostly 5.10-5.11 thin face climbing leads to a reachy, bouldery crux sequence ending in a downclimb past two bolts.

current.approach: Same East Face approach as Liberty Crack: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. The route begins in the same general area as Liberty Crack and the Independence Route on the lower East Face — verify you're at the correct start, since several route lines begin within a short distance of each other along the base talus.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the ground between Thin Red Line and the Independence Route
current.descent: Live Free or Die climbs the East Face for 8 pitches to M&M Ledge (roughly mid-height), then shares its final 3-4 pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles in the small sizes up to #0.5 Camalot, singles from #0.75 to #3, small wires, a 70 m rope, and numerous slings/quickdraws for the bolted sections.
current.pro_needs: Pitches 1-3 and 5 are mostly bolt-protected and need only a couple of cams; pitch 4 has two bolts at its crux but needs a cam rack for the rest, as do the thin crack and splitter pitches higher up.

name: South Route
beta: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own — parties reach it only by first completing several days of the Ptarmigan Traverse's off-trail, glaciated high route, then scrambling from a camp near Lizard Col. The summit push itself is straightforward (class 3) once you're on site; the real crux of the route is the multi-day glacier approach to get there.
overview: A remote, seldom-visited summit on the divide between the Cascade Pass and Dome Peak country, Lizard Mountain rises above the White Rock Lakes basin along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse -- one of the North Cascades' premier glaciated high routes. Most parties encounter it as a half-day side-scramble from a White Rock Lakes camp (reached via Lizard Pass), roughly three to four days into a north-to-south traverse from Cascade Pass; there is no dedicated trailhead or day-hike approach. The Class 3 heather-and-slab summit rewards the effort with sweeping views over the LeConte and South Cascade Glaciers (the latter a long-term USGS benchmark glacier used for decades of glacier mass-balance research) toward Dome Peak and Glacier Peak.

current.approach: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own. It is climbed from a camp at White Rock Lakes, which parties reach from the north over the first half of the Ptarmigan Traverse and leave the same way. Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of the Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount. The maintained trail switchbacks about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft up to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last built tread of the trip. From the pass a climbers' path traverses south-southeast across the flank of Mixup Peak to the Cache Glacier; rope up for the glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then drop to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), the usual first camp. Beyond the lake the Red Ledge crosses the cliff band, and a roped crossing of the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the gap beside Spider Mountain and down to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft). From there climb onto the Le Conte Glacier, work around Sentinel Peak, cross the broad South Cascade Glacier and top out at Lizard Col (~6,800 ft) on Lizard's south ridge, then descend to White Rock Lakes (~6,200 ft). From camp, regain the col and follow the south ridge roughly 600 vertical feet to the summit, a short but loose Class 2-3 scramble; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks. Most parties take three days to reach White Rock Lakes, and the whole outing is about 35 miles round trip with some 11,000 ft of cumulative gain. The southern approach from the Downey Creek Trailhead starts with a road walk at present: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at milepost 12, about 8 miles below the trailhead; check status before planning on it.
approach_variant_names: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed at milepost 12)
current.descent: Reverse the south ridge from the summit to Lizard Col. It is loose Class 2 the whole way and needs no rappels; many parties use the west ridge as an alternative way back down to the col. From the col, drop to camp at White Rock Lakes, then retrace the approach north: across the South Cascade Glacier and around Sentinel Peak on the Le Conte Glacier to Yang Yang Lakes, over the Middle Cascade Glacier and along the Red Ledge to Kool-Aid Lake, then up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier and across to Cascade Pass, and down the trail to the Cascade River Road. The glaciers carry the same crevasse hazard on the way out as on the way in, and most parties take three days from White Rock Lakes back to the car.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the class 3 scramble itself. A rope per team for crossing the Le Conte, South Cascade, and other glaciers between Cascade Pass and Lizard Col.
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are almost entirely about the glacier approach rather than the summit scramble: a rope for each glacier-travel team, a full crevasse-rescue kit, and a helmet for rockfall/icefall exposure along the traverse.
bivy: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
current.rope_note: No route-specific trip report found for this remote Chelan County peak near Dome Peak; gear inferred from the Class 3 rating — standard talus/rock scrambling, ice axe recommended if snow lingers on approach slopes.

name: Lone Wolf
beta: Lone Wolf follows the obvious, continuous bolt line up The Obelisk's main face for two pitches of 5.10a climbing to bolted chain anchors. It is currently the only documented route on this formation, established in 2020 as part of a small, still-developing crag alongside the neighboring Sofa King Buttress.
overview: A 2-pitch, 200-ft bolted sport line straight up the main face of The Obelisk, a distinctive pinnacle-like rock embossment protruding from the mountainside in Silver Basin near Snoqualmie Pass.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
current.descent: From the top of pitch 2, rappel (or lower with a sufficiently long rope) to the bolted chain anchor atop pitch 1, then rappel again to the base of the face. No walk-off descent has been documented for this route.
current.detailed_rack: A standard sport rack of quickdraws sized for a 2-pitch bolted line; bring enough draws to cover the longer pitch plus the anchor. Bolted chain anchors at the top of each pitch allow rappelling or lowering — no trad gear is needed for protection.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted sport protection throughout; no gear placements required.
current.rope_note: Two bolted pitches of about 30 m each; a single 60 m rope rappels or lowers from the chain anchor atop each pitch.

name: Southwest Slope - Southeast Ridge
beta: Recorded in Sept 2000: approach from the White River Trailhead via Boulder Creek, over a sheepherder's trail through Boulder, Clark, Luahna and Chalangin basins, to a high camp near 5,800 ft below Luahna. The summit push climbs class 2 ledges on the south face onto the ridge, crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side beneath the summit, then finishes with class 3 scrambling straight up to the top.
overview: An alternate approach up Luahna's southwest slope, gained via the White River side and Boulder/Clark/Luahna basins, finishing up class 2 ledges and ridge to an exposed class 3+ traverse beneath the summit and a final class 3 scramble to the top.

current.approach: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft) follow the White River Trail and Boulder Creek to a ford/camp around 3,700 ft, then continue up into Boulder Basin to a high camp near 5,800 ft. From high camp, traverse via Clark Basin and Luahna Basin (crossing a faint sheepherder's trail with significant side-hilling) to reach the base of Luahna's southwest slope.
approach_variant_names: Boulder Basin high camp and the sheepherder's trail through four cirques
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the class 3 section, re-cross the exposed class 3+ traverse beneath the summit, and descend the class 2 south-face ledges back to the ridge and basin below. From there retrace the sheepherder's-trail traverse back through Luahna, Clark, and Boulder basins to the high camp, then follow Boulder Creek and the White River Trail back to the trailhead.
bivy: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River

name: Luna Glacier
beta: From Luna Cirque, climb steepening glacier/snow up the hanging glacier below the peak (the technical crux, and reportedly impassable late in the season) to a notch, then transition to rock. Two to three pitches of easy 5th-class slab climbing lead up to the summit ridge; stay off the towers on the south side and climb the final 25-ft summit block directly. Descend by rappelling where possible and downclimbing the route back to the glacier.
overview: The Luna Glacier route is Phantom Peak's original 1940 first-ascent line, named for the small hanging glacier that lies just south of the peak above Luna Cirque (not an officially named glacier, but the moniker stuck). It's a moderate snow-and-easy-rock outing by Pickets standards — Grade II, Easy 5th class — but its remoteness and glacier crux keep it a rarely repeated route.

current.approach: Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical approach follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake (the Ross Lake Resort water taxi, charged per boat, cuts about 6 miles off the hike) up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque — the bushwhack is a notoriously miserable fight through flies, devil's club, willows, and alder. Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off that same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead — parties continue on the maintained trail a mile to a mile and a half past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail there to follow the Access Creek drainage (with an occasional bootpath) up into the cirque — a longer but far less brutal line than Luna Creek.
approach_variant_names: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek into Luna Cirque, rather than the Luna Creek bushwhack
current.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or rappel off the summit block, reverse the slab pitches to the top of the highest snowfield, downclimb the rock step, and descend the hanging glacier roped and protected with pickets/flukes back into Luna Cirque and high camp.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack: runners and a few pieces of trad gear (small-to-medium) for the class 4-5 slab pitches, plus pickets for the hanging glacier and bergschrund below.
rack: Light rack: a few cams and nuts (runners and a few pieces of gear)
A few snow pickets or flukes for the glacier crux
Single rope for rappelling/downclimbing off the summit block
current.pro_needs: Protection for the rock is simply runners and a few pieces of gear, supplemented by standard glacier-travel protection for the snow/ice approach.
current.rope_note: Grade II, 4 pitches/400ft, easy 5th class rock above a hanging glacier crux (may be impassable late season). Carry ice axe/crampons for the glacier + light rock rack. Helmets required.

name: Southwest Ridge
beta: Access from Luna Cirque via Access Creek, ascend steep gullies to southeast ridge, traverse to southwest ridge with exposed Class 3 summit traverse on loose rock. Crux is 5 feet exposed between false and true summit.
overview: Luna Peak is the highest summit of the Picket Range and a coveted viewpoint over the savage skyline of the Southern and Northern Pickets. First climbed in September 1938 by Bill Cox and Will F. Thompson, it is also one of Washington's highest-prominence peaks (required for the WA 2,000+ ft prominence list). No maintained trail reaches the mountain — the standard line is a long, remote, largely off-trail approach via Big Beaver and Access Creek, making this one of the more committing 'moderate' summits in the Cascades despite its modest Class 3 technical grade.

current.approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134), cross Ross Dam and work around the lake to the Big Beaver Trail, or save about 7 miles by taking the lake boat shuttle to Big Beaver landing. Follow Big Beaver Trail past Luna Camp, roughly 10 miles up from the landing, and leave it about 1.5 miles beyond the camp at a big cairn on the left. Drop through forest to Big Beaver Creek, ford it since logs are not dependable, then traverse southwest through alder thickets to the head of Access Creek, crossing it near 3900 ft and camping in the meadow near 4200 ft. From there climb about 2000 ft of loose gully to the col that opens onto the southwest ridge, and make an ascending traverse to the next col at the edge of the ridge, where the climbing starts.
approach_variant_names: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
current.descent: Descend the way you came. From the summit, work back along the ramps and ledges on the southeast side to the false summit, then downclimb the class 3 rock of the southwest ridge to the col. The step between the two summits is very exposed and a fall there would be fatal, so move carefully and avoid wet rock. From the col, retrace the traverse to the upper col and descend the gully to the Access Creek meadows, which becomes a loose rock pile late in the season, so stay close together or out of each other's fall line and wear helmets. Then bushwhack back to Big Beaver Creek, ford it, and walk the Big Beaver trail out to the Ross Lake landing.
current.detailed_rack: Optional: 50-60m rope for belayed crux; many solo. Minimal rock gear.
current.pro_needs: Varies by experience. Single 50m rope with harness/slings for crux. Self-rescue knowledge essential.
current.rope_note: Standard SE approach ascends scree/rubble climber's right to a steep snow-filled chute onto Luna's SE shoulder and Luna Col (7,200 ft); ice axe and microspikes/aluminum crampons needed year-round for the snow chute. The route itself is usually unroped, but some parties carry a short rope for the glaciated approach snowfields and the Class 3-4 summit block shared with the South Ridge route.

name: East Ridge
beta: Broken rock, past a slab section and up another small section of featured rock to the summit. Three large installed bolts aid navigation, and multiple easy variations are available.
overview: A short, easy final pitch of broken rock and slab to Lundin's summit from the saddle between Lundin and East Lundin, reached via a considerably longer approach over Red Pass.

current.approach: From the PCT parking lot at I-90 Exit 52, hike the Pacific Crest Trail 2 miles to the Commonwealth Creek trail junction, then continue about 2.5 more miles, passing Red Mountain and Red Pond, to Red Pass. From Red Pass follow the climbers' path west to the saddle between Lundin Peak and East Lundin.
current.descent: Rappel from the installed bolts on the ridge or downclimb the same broken rock and slabs to the saddle between Lundin Peak and East Lundin Peak. From the saddle, follow the climbers' path over to Red Pass, then take the Commonwealth Creek trail down to the PCT and out to the parking lot at the Snoqualmie Pass exit. Allow about two hours from East Lundin to the car. The three large bolts are best treated as landmarks and a rappel anchor to back up. In June and July a rope of 35 to 40 m reaches easy scrambling ground from the east-ridge rappel; a 30 m rope falls short of it.
current.detailed_rack: A lightweight alpine rack emphasizing smaller pieces, or alternatively 3 quickdraws and anchor material to use the three installed bolts.
current.pro_needs: Small gear, or quickdraws for the fixed bolts.

name: West Ridge
beta: The West Ridge is a compact, sub-1,000-foot ridge climb rated Easy 5th/Grade II. Climbers gain the ridge crest from a notch, then move over generally sound blocky rock, mostly Class 3-4 scrambling with a crux slabby depression rated Class 4/5.0 guarding the final approach to the summit. It's frequently used as a first alpine rock climb, though route-finding, some cliffing, and loose talus mean it should not be treated as a casual scramble.
overview: Lundin Peak is a jagged, three-horned summit — the true summit sits at the eastern end of the spine — on the ridge connecting Snoqualmie Mountain (6,278 ft) to Red Mountain, immediately north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Formerly named 'Snoqualmie Little Sister,' it was renamed in 1931 to honor district forest ranger John Lundin. Short approaches from I-90 and a mix of scrambling/low-5th rock make it one of the most popular half-day alpine objectives near Seattle, but the summit block is genuinely technical: expect Class 4 and low-5th (about 5.0) climbing with real exposure on the final pitch, not a walk-up scramble.

current.approach: Two standard ways to reach the base of the West Ridge, both converging on the ridge's low-point notch around 5,800 ft where the technical climbing starts. (1) Commonwealth/Lundin Basin approach: from the PCT-North/Commonwealth Basin trailhead off Alpental Rd (elev. ~3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within about half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use-trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth forest for roughly 1.7 mi as the valley opens into the basin. Near 4,200 ft, leave the main Red Pass/Commonwealth Basin tread and cut left (west), contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir (snow early season, scree/talus by late summer) up Lundin's steep south face to gain the West Ridge at the obvious saddle/notch. This leg runs roughly 3.5-4 miles one-way with about 2,800 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours. Commonwealth Creek is a reliable water source in the lower basin but nothing is dependable once you're up in Lundin Basin, so top off early. Hazards: the south-face couloir is prone to wet-slide/sluffing in afternoon sun and wants an axe (crampons if firm) in early season; the basin traverse can be brushy, boulder-hop route-finding once snow melts out late in the season. (2) Cave Ridge/Alpental approach (faster, and the better late-season option since it skirts the brushy lower basin): park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained 'Snoqualmie Mountain' climbers' trail beginning about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder to an unsigned split around 4,600 ft where paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge, and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge/Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest (staying on the Commonwealth Basin/north side) to the West Ridge notch. About 2.5-3 miles one-way, ~2,800-3,000 ft gain; trip reports clock roughly 2.5-4 hours trailhead-to-ridge-base. No reliable water past the trailhead. Hazards: exposed, sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse under Cave Ridge, and an early-season snow traverse that can warrant an axe.
approach_variant_names: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
current.descent: Most parties reverse the West Ridge: from the true (west) summit, downclimb the class 3-4 ridge crest back toward the notch/saddle used on the way up, staying on the north side of the crest per the standard line and reversing the short crux step (a ~6 ft downclimb at a minor notch). Many parties downclimb this cleanly, but a single short rappel (roughly 15 m/50 ft, well within a 30 m single-rope length) is commonly used here instead, especially in wet conditions or with less experienced climbers — anchors are natural (slung horns/blocks or a small nut/cam placement backed by a cordelette), not bolted; there's no fixed hardware on this route. From the saddle, either reverse the ascent couloir into Lundin Basin (a fast glissade of up to 1,200-1,500 ft when it's still snow-filled, typically only reliable early season) or walk scree/talus down toward the Red-Lundin col to pick up the use trail back into Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. An alternative some parties use is descending the East Ridge instead: scramble down the crest about 100 ft to the top of a small cliff band, then make one single-rope rappel (30 m is sufficient; natural tree/horn anchors — the ridge has plenty of trees to sling) down to easy ledges, continuing to a notch in the ridge crest from which an early-season glissade or scramble rejoins the standard route in Lundin/Commonwealth Basin. This option requires either looping back on foot into Commonwealth Basin or a car shuttle/hitch between the Alpental and PCT-North trailheads, since the two approaches start at different lots. Bottom line for planning: expect zero to one short rappel (under 15 m, single rope, natural gear anchors — no bolts) — conditions and party comfort level determine whether it's downclimbed or rapped. Total descent to the trailhead runs roughly 2-2.5 hours. To make a loop, descend the east ridge from July to September: a short class 2-3 walk leads to the rappel anchors (about 35 to 40 m to easy ground), then a boot path drops to the saddle with East Lundin and over to Red Pass.
current.detailed_rack: Small alpine rack (6-7 pieces), 30 m rope, 3 runners with carabiners, slings for trees.
current.pro_needs: Light trad rack for the short Class 4/5.0 sections and tree/gear anchors for the rappel; the route is short enough that protection needs are minimal compared to the routefinding and loose-rock hazard.

name: North Face
beta: From a camp at Pelton Basin, ascend easy slopes, then a steep couloir and the Yawning Glacier up to the Magic-Pelton col (~6,480 ft). From the col, traverse back and cross the head of the glacier to reach the north face, then climb about 600 ft of steep class 4 rock to a notch immediately northwest of the summit, from which the true summit is a short scramble away.
overview: A glacier-approach line up Magic Mountain's north side via the Yawning Glacier, finishing with a distinct 600 ft class 4 rock face to a notch just northwest of the summit.

current.approach: Same trailhead and Cascade Pass approach as the South Ridge route, but continue toward Pelton Basin (rather than Kool-Aid Lake) as the camp for this route.
approach_variant_names: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier, then west across the glacier head to the face
current.descent: Downclimb the class 4 north face back to the head of the Yawning Glacier, cross back to the Magic-Pelton col, and descend the couloir/glacier to Pelton Basin.
current.detailed_rack: A rope for the Yawning Glacier and couloir; rock rack for the class 4 face is minimal (natural gear/slings).
current.pro_needs: Standard glacier travel protection (pickets/screws as conditions dictate) plus a light rack for optional protection on the class 4 face.

name: Northeast Couloir
beta: The Northeast Couloir is the snow alternative to the North Face and shares its entire approach. From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier (which spans roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft), and follow the glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. From there, instead of traversing west to the north face, take the couloir directly to the summit — the published description allows for either rock or snow depending on the year and the season. Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir and describe it as consistently steep but wide, winding down Magic Mountain's shoulder, with a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 degrees at the very top. Expect rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on both sides and heavy sluffing once the sun gets on it — the lower section can turn into a chute for falling debris. This is an early-start, frozen-conditions objective.
overview: A snow line on the peak's northeast flank: follow the North Face approach up the Yawning Glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col, then take the couloir directly to the summit on rock or snow. Known to skiers as the Banana Couloir, with a consistently steep fall-line.

current.approach: Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead (~3,600 ft). Hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), then cross the pass and descend east toward the Stehekin side; Pelton Basin Camp is about 0.5 miles downhill and east of the pass, 4.9 miles and 1,800 ft of gain from the trailhead including the 0.2-mile camp spur. From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier, rope up, and follow the glacier southwest to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft between Magic Mountain and Pelton Peak. The couloir rises from the glacier on the northeast side of the peak; ski parties also access this cirque from the Cascade Pass side via the Yawning Glacier without dropping to Pelton Basin.
approach_variant_names: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier to the col, then straight up the line
current.descent: There are two sane exits. Reversing the line — downclimbing or skiing the couloir to the Yawning Glacier and back over the Magic–Pelton Col to Pelton Basin — is the direct option and the one ski parties take, but it means being in a sun-exposed couloir on the way down, which is exactly the condition every trip report warns about. The alternative is to walk off the peak's standard South Ridge: downclimb the Class 3-4 ledges around the summit tower, regain the false summit via the 80 ft dirty gully, follow the south ridge to the Magic–Hurry-up col and descend 1,000 ft to Kool-Aid Lake, then out over Cache Col — much longer, but it avoids the couloir entirely. Choose before you leave the col, because the two put you on opposite sides of the mountain, and match the choice to the freeze: if the overnight freeze was poor, the South Ridge is the right answer.
current.detailed_rack: This is a snow route, so the rack is snow and glacier hardware rather than rock gear. Two or three pickets cover belays and running protection on the steepest ground; one or two ice screws are worth having for the firm crust reported near the top and for a hard bergschrund lip on the glacier. A 40-50 m rope handles both roped glacier travel and any belayed pitches in the couloir. If you expect the lean-year rock finish, add a small selection of nuts and long slings for block anchors on the broken gneiss.
current.pro_needs: On snow, protection is pickets and, where the crust is hard, screws — most parties solo the lower and middle couloir and belay or run out pickets on the top 100-200 ft where the angle reaches 50 degrees. The Yawning Glacier below requires roped travel and a functioning crevasse-rescue system. In a lean year the finish is rock rather than snow, and then the route needs a handful of nuts and long slings for slung-block belays on broken gneiss, with the caveat that there are no fixed anchors anywhere on this peak.

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: Approach as for the South Ridge route, then ascend easy slopes southwest of Magic Mountain to the base of the ridge/face. Climb steep rock and finally an easy chimney to a notch northwest of the summit (the same notch reached by the North Face route), then traverse and climb the short remaining distance to the summit via the NW face.
overview: A class 4 alternative to the North Face that gains the same summit notch from the southwest side of the mountain via steep rock and an easy chimney.

current.approach: Same Cascade Pass Trailhead / Cascade Pass approach as the South Ridge route, then continue to easy slopes on Magic Mountain's southwest side rather than dropping to Kool-Aid Lake.
approach_variant_names: Kool-Aid Lake side: easy slopes southwest of the peak to the chimney and the notch
current.descent: Descend the South Ridge: downclimb the Class 3-4 ledges around the east side of the summit tower, regain the false summit up the short gully, and follow the ridge down to the Magic-Hurry-up col above Kool-Aid Lake. To reverse the route instead, go back down the short NW-face scramble to the notch, then downclimb the chimney and steep rock to the easy slopes below.
current.detailed_rack: Light rock rack/slings for the steep rock and chimney section.
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse and improvised. The steep rock below the chimney is the section where a rope is most likely to come out, but the broken gneiss takes cams poorly and you will get more from slinging features than from placing gear. Most competent parties move together or solo the Class 4, using the rope only for a nervous partner or for a retreat. The chimney is described as easy and generally needs nothing. The genuinely protectable moments on the day are on the Cache Glacier during the approach and exit.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Slopes
beta: From Kool-Aid Lake, descend about 600 ft on the Ptarmigan Traverse path, then traverse and climb to a 7,100 ft col east of the lake. From that col, ascend the South Ridge on heather and rock (Class 3) toward a false summit roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true summit. Drop off the false summit and cross broken, exposed Class 3-4 ledges/gully on the east side of the summit tower to reach the true summit; fresh snow can force a detour into the summit moat.
overview: Set above the head of Cascade Pass near Spider-Formidable country, Magic Mountain (7,610 ft) is a rewarding scramble usually combined with a backcountry camp in the basin below. The South Ridge / Southeast Slopes standard route leaves Cascade Pass on a climber's path that traverses heather and talus below Mixup Peak's east slopes to the small Cache Glacier and Cache Col (6,900 ft), then descends a rising traverse SSE to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), a popular camp at the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse. From camp the route climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-up Peak, follows an easy heather ridge to a false summit (roughly 300 ft SE of, and slightly lower than, the true summit), then drops about 80 ft to gain Class 3-4 broken, corkscrewing ledges on the NE face leading to the true summit. First climbed in 1938 by Calder Bressler, Ray Clough, Bill Cox, and Tom Myers.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), follow the Cascade Pass Trail — a well-graded, heavily switchbacked National Park trail — 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,360-5,400 ft), the low notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. This section is on-trail, well-marked, and passable by early-to-mid summer once the switchbacks melt out; it's also the most crowded stretch since it's a popular day hike in its own right. At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on the east flank of Mixup Peak. This climber's trail is intermittent and route-finding becomes more important in early season when it's snow-covered. Continue the traverse to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft), then ascend moderate snow slopes (up to about 35 degrees) to Cache Col (6,900-6,960 ft); the glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying for the snow slope depending on season and firmness. From Cache Col, descend roughly 600 ft on a climber's path with a descending traverse to the southeast, dropping to Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft), the standard camp/bivy area for Magic Mountain and the broader Ptarmigan Traverse. From Kool-Aid Lake, the final approach climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree slopes to the col (~7,100 ft) separating Magic Mountain from neighboring Hurry Up Peak, which is where the South Ridge proper begins. There is reliable water at Kool-Aid Lake and seasonal snowmelt along the traverse, but none on the upper ridge itself. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the trailhead and a backcountry camping permit is required from North Cascades National Park for overnight stays at Kool-Aid Lake; most parties treat this as a 2-day trip with a camp at the lake rather than a car-to-car push given the off-trail navigation. Water at Kool-Aid Lake is plentiful in early August but tastes stale, so treat it.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line down the South Ridge. From the true summit (7,610 ft), climb back down the Class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew the east side of the summit tower, then climb back up the roughly 80 ft dirty gully to the false summit (about 300 ft southeast of the true summit) before continuing down the easy heather/scree of the South Ridge to the Magic Mountain-Hurry Up col. This corkscrew section is the technical crux of the whole outing — loose, broken rock with real exposure — and is where the route's single rappel comes in: many parties downclimb it as Class 3-4 with a spotting belay, but a short single-rope rappel (roughly 50-80 ft, well within a 30m or 60m single strand, or a doubled 30m rope) off a natural anchor — a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there are no bolts or fixed hardware reported on this remote, lightly-traveled summit — is commonly used by parties wanting to avoid down-climbing the loose ledges, especially in wet or snowy conditions. From the col, retrace the approach: down to Kool-Aid Lake, back up and over Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes and the Mixup Peak traverse to Cascade Pass, then out the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock on the corkscrew ledges and the upper gully, and for soft/rotten snow on the Cache Glacier descent later in the day — this is a route best started early to avoid downclimbing softened snow on the return.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack of small to mid cams and a few nuts suffices for the summit moves.
current.pro_needs: Very light; protection is mostly for the final scramble.

name: Southwest Cirque
beta: Approach as for the South Ridge route to the cirque southwest of the summit. Climb any of the heathery gullies at the north or northeast head of the cirque to gain the summit ridge, then finish to the top.
overview: A class 3-4 scramble up heathery gullies from the cirque southwest of the summit, sharing the South Ridge route's approach.

current.approach: Same Cascade Pass Trailhead / Cascade Pass / Kool-Aid Lake approach as the South Ridge route, diverting into the cirque southwest of the summit rather than continuing to the Hurry-up col.
current.descent: Descend the South Ridge: downclimb the Class 3-4 ledges around the east side of the summit tower, regain the false summit, and follow the ridge down to the Magic-Hurry-up col above Kool-Aid Lake. Alternatively, reverse the heathery gully back down into the southwest cirque.
current.detailed_rack: Minimal — an unroped heather/rock scramble.
current.pro_needs: Effectively none — this is a protection-free route by design. The gullies are heather, dirt and broken gneiss; there is nothing to place and nothing fixed. Parties that want security should bring a short rope for hand-lines and rely on slung heather clumps and blocks, understanding that these are psychological rather than real anchors. The one place a rope earns its weight is the Cache Glacier on the approach and exit, where roped travel and a crevasse-rescue system are appropriate.

name: Tepeh Towers
beta: Climbed almost exclusively as a quick side objective from Eldorado's East Ridge camp — glacier travel to the base, a moat crossing, one short low-5th pitch, then scrambling to the top; round trip from camp is well under 2 hours.
overview: A very short, easy alpine rock add-on to an Eldorado Peak trip: one low-5th-class pitch and some scrambling to a minor summit visible across the icecap from camp.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) up the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. From the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600 ft), rope up and walk about 45 minutes north-northwest across the glacier to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arête that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.
approach_variant_names: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb or rappel from a fixed rappel station directly below the top, landing back on the glacier for the return traverse to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A single light rack to 2 inches plus a handful of slings is enough for the one short pitch; the rest is glacier and scrambling gear.
current.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed — one short low-5th pitch with a small rack.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: West Ridge
beta: From Holden Pass (the saddle shared with Bonanza Peak), gain the ridge via a series of gullies, scrambling on the right (south) side of the crest and repeating this pattern upward. The rock is loose/crumbly throughout, so route-finding by cairn is common. A short, exposed Class 4 section with good holds is encountered just below the summit; a fixed rappel anchor has been observed there for parties who prefer to rope up rather than downclimb it.
overview: The peak's standard/easiest line: climbs the crest of Martin Peak's west ridge from Holden Pass to the summit, mostly Class 3 scrambling on loose schist with one short, well-featured Class 4 step just below the top.

current.approach: All approaches to Martin Peak begin at Holden Village: take the Lake Chelan ferry (Chelan Boat Company's Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express) from Chelan or Fields Point Landing to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up an 11-mile gravel road (12 switchbacks) into Holden Village. FSR 8301 and the Lucerne dock have been closed to all vehicle and foot traffic since the December 2025 mudslides and the bus is not running, so check with the Chelan Ranger District before planning on this access. From Holden, follow the Railroad Creek Trail up-valley and continue to Holden Pass, the saddle between Bonanza and Martin Peaks, to reach the base of the west ridge.
approach_variant_names: Holden Village to Holden Pass, then east up the ridge
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line down the west ridge, following cairns back through the loose gully sections. The fixed rappel anchor near the summit allows a short rappel past the crux Class 4 step for parties who don't want to downclimb it; the rest of the descent is downclimbed. Expect the same loose-rock hazard on the way down as on the way up.
current.detailed_rack: A single 30-60m rope with a light rack — a handful of small-to-mid cams/nuts and a few slings — is enough to protect the roped Class 3-4 sections and the exposed Class 4 crux gully below the summit. Many strong scrambling parties climb the route unroped in dry conditions.
rack: Light rack: a few small-to-mid cams and nuts
A few slings for natural anchors (horns, chockstones, trees)
30-60m rope for the crux gully / exposed step near the summit
current.pro_needs: Most parties travel unroped; a rope and a few slings/a picket cover the single optional rappel near the summit for those who don't want to downclimb the Class 4 step.
bivy: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
current.rope_note: Carry a rope and a few slings. This route's own gear list holds both, for the optional rappel near the summit: there is a fixed anchor up there that lets a party past the crux Class 4 step without downclimbing it. The rest of the west ridge is Class 3 scrambling on loose schist and is not roped, and the rock is crumbly the whole way, so a helmet matters more than a rack here.

name: Marvin's Ear
beta: 800 feet, Grade III 5.10b, with well-protected cruxes though bolts are spaced further apart on easier (5.9-and-under) terrain. Prior to this route, only one other technical line (Starshot Ridge, 5.8, established 1981) existed on Vega Tower, and the west ridge itself was unclimbed until 2016/2017.
overview: Marvin's Ear climbs the skyline ridge of Vega Tower — the sub-summit just east of Vega North Tower/Eros Tower — via a fully bolted 800-ft, 7-pitch alpine sport line (Grade III, 5.10b) through hard metaconglomerate rock. It was the first technical route up Vega Tower's west ridge proper (the only prior technical line, Starshot Ridge 5.8, was established in 1981 on a different aspect); climbing gets progressively more exposed as it skirts over the north face in the upper pitches.

current.approach: Same Sunrise Mine Trail approach as Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining: follow the trail roughly 2.5 miles to the last major switchback at about 4,300 ft, then leave the trail for a cairned talus traverse heading northeast across two talus fields toward the Vega towers (shared with the other Vega North Tower routes). Where the traverse for Mile High Club and Beyond Redlining continues toward the base of the main west face, Marvin's Ear branches off into a gully to the right (east) of Vega North Tower. Follow this gully up through cedar and heather — vegetated, sometimes loose ground — to a notch on the skyline ridge. From the notch, the last bit to the pitch-one belay involves loose 3rd-class terrain with some exposed 4th-class moves, landing on a grassy ledge that serves as the first belay. Because this gully approach is steeper and more vegetated than the open talus used by Mile High Club, expect a slower, more route-finding-dependent final approach, and be cautious of loose blocks in the gully, especially with parties above.
approach_variant_names: Sunrise Mine Trail, then the east-side gully
current.descent: Marvin's Ear is rappelled back down its own line (not via Mile High Club). Bolted anchors are set roughly 30m apart along the route, so a single 60m rope will come up short in places — bring a 70m rope, which lets you link some of the 30m-spaced stations into longer raps and reduces the rappel count to roughly four full-length raps rather than seven pitch-by-pitch rappels. Beta from parties who've done the descent numbers them R1 through R4: R1 has notable rope friction on the pull; R2 requires looking right near the end of the rope to find the next station; R3 trends straight down; R4 is straightforward. One notable trap: partway down you'll see a shiny pair of rap chains that looks like the anchor — it isn't the one to use. Instead traverse left to find a hidden bolt behind a rock, then continue left to the actual bolted rappel anchor (no chains), which is the correct line down. Watch for loose rock and rope-catching pinches throughout the descent, consistent with the route's overall character on this face.
current.detailed_rack: Quickdraws plus several alpine draws; 70m rope recommended for both leading and the rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted; quickdraws and a few alpine draws cover the whole route. A 70m rope is needed both to climb the longer pitches and to rappel.
bivy: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
current.rope_note: A 70 m rope is required rather than preferred: the bolted anchors sit roughly 30 m apart, so a 60 m leaves the rappels short. Quickdraws plus several alpine draws, and a helmet. The line is fully bolted but the spacing is not uniform - four bolts on pitch 1 and six on pitch 2, nine or ten through pitches 4 to 7 where the climbing is sustained at 5.9 to 5.10b, and pitch 3 is a 5.0 walk along ledges with a single bolt between the belays. The descent rappels the route itself on the 70, linking the 30 m stations into roughly four full-length raps.

name: West Route
beta: From the Trinity/Buck Creek Trailhead, follow the Chiwawa River Trail north about 4 miles to the unsigned, unmaintained 'Massie Lake' way-trail (an old sheepherder driveway marked by axe/burn blazes on trees) and climb steeply to Massie Lake. From the lake, gain the ridge above and continue cross-country toward the summit, bypassing a false summit before reaching the true top. The line is difficult to follow, brushy, and has claimed parties onto unwanted 4th-class terrain when off-route; a Aug-2024 trip report logged 14.75 miles round trip, about 5,400' of gain, and 7 hours car-to-car via a non-standard east-ridge/south-ridge variant, noting the descent line is easy to lose.
overview: Massie Peak is a remote, seldom-visited summit on the ridge above Massie Lake in the Phelps Creek/Chiwawa River high country of the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has no maintained trail to its summit and is usually climbed as a side-trip from longer backcountry loops through Buck Creek Pass, High Pass, Liberty Cap, and neighboring Chiwawa Mountain, reached via the unmaintained 'Massie Lake High Route' — an old sheepherder's path — rather than any signed trail.

current.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (~2,820 ft, at the end of Chiwawa River/Chiwawa Valley Road, Forest Road 6200, reached via Coles Corner and Hwy 207), pick up the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and follow it upstream through forest for roughly 4 miles. Watch the left (west) side of the trail for an 'M' blazed/carved into a tree — this marks the unsigned, unmaintained sheepherder's path up to Massie Lake, and it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Ford the Chiwawa River at this point (can run cold and pushy with snowmelt into early summer; trekking poles help, expect wet feet) and pick up the old sheep-drive trail, which climbs steeply via a mix of tree blazes and intermittent boot-track for about 2 miles to Massie Lake (about 5,900 ft), a clear trout-holding tarn with a couple of established campsites. There is essentially no reliable water between the river ford and the lake, so fill up at the Chiwawa. From Massie Lake, continue on the faint sheep/game-trail tread of the Massie Lake High Route, contouring northwest roughly 1.5 miles toward Pass No Pass, then leave that trail and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge. Follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block — to the 7,533 ft summit. The main hazard throughout is route-finding: the sheepherder path disappears in places, blazes thin out above treeline, and the entire line beyond the Chiwawa River Trail is off-trail, unsigned, and easy to lose in flat light — bring a map/GPS track. Snow and ice can linger on shaded sections of the high route and ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe for trips before mid-July.
approach_variant_names: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the west ridge (Class 2-3, some loose rock underfoot) back to the point where you gained it from the Massie Lake High Route, rejoin that faint tread and follow it back southeast to Massie Lake, then descend the steep sheepherder path back down to the Chiwawa River ford and out the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 to Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route — there are no fixed anchors reported on Massie Peak's west ridge or the approach gully, consistent with its Class 2-3 scrambling character. The trickiest part of the descent is simply staying on the correct (badly faded) line: the sheep trail is easy to lose both up in the high-route traverse and on the steep drop back to the river, and a mistaken line can dead-end in cliff bands or brush. Some parties instead continue past Massie Lake and pick a 'route of least resistance' down open slopes directly to Buck Creek Trail when linking Massie Peak with neighboring summits (Mount Cleator, Helmet Butte, Liberty Cap) on a multi-day loop, but for a straightforward out-and-back on the West Route, reversing the ascent line described above is the standard descent.
bivy: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
current.rope_note: Nothing route-specific has been published for this line, so take what follows as what the grade and the terrain imply rather than as tested beta. At Class 2-3 there is no rope and no rack: the descent reverses the ascent, and no fixed anchors have been reported anywhere on the west ridge or the approach gully. What the route does take is an ice axe early season, trekking poles, and a helmet - the ridge crest is loose and has short exposed Class 3 moves. The real difficulty is staying on a badly faded sheep path, not the climbing.

name: Southwest Scramble
beta: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes and on past Lake Viviane to the flat ground between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes (~7,000 ft). Leave the trail there and head south-southeast toward the ridge connecting to McClellan, keeping west of the distinct rock tower known as 'The Prong.' Gain the ridge on Class 2-3 talus/slabs, cross to the south side, and finish with a short, exposed Class 3 (some report low Class 4) scramble up the summit block, easiest from its southeast side; descend the same way.
overview: McClellan Peak forms the high, sprawling rampart on the southeast side of the Enchantments, a granite massif with substantial prominence that rises above the Snow Lakes and Nada Lake basins. It sits about 1.3 miles east of Little Annapurna and 1.6 miles southwest of The Temple, and was first climbed July 5, 1946 by Ken Prestrud, Keith Rankin, and William Herston. The mountain is composed of Late Cretaceous tonalitic plutons; its broad summit ridge carries subsidiary towers (the Prong, and 'the Pawn' — first of the Chessmen) that offer 5th-class rock climbing for parties who want more than the standard Class 3 scramble to the true summit.

current.approach: From Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 4.2–4.3 miles west to the Snow Lakes Trailhead and parking area on the south side of the road (~1,350 ft). Start on the Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553, which climbs steadily through forest along Icicle Creek/Snow Creek drainage. About 5.3 miles in you pass Nada Lake, with a loud waterfall/creek blast just above it that's a reliable water source; continue to Lower and Upper Snow Lakes, where a logjam between the two lakes is a known crossing hazard (especially at high water or in the dark on an alpine start). Beyond the Snow Lakes the trail (now a rougher climbers' path) switchbacks steeply up into the core Enchantments basin, passing Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes — by this point you've covered roughly 9–10 miles and gained most of the route's elevation. At the flat, open area at ~7,000 ft between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes, leave the maintained trail and head south-southeast, aiming for McClellan Ridge and staying west of a distinctive rock tower known as "the Prong." Ascend steep talus, scree, or snow (depending on season — often firm/icy in late summer and fall, so an axe/microspikes are worth carrying) to gain the ridge crest. This upper section has no reliable water and involves real route-finding; a permit is required to camp overnight in the core Enchantments zone (May 15-Oct 31).
approach_variant_names: Snow Lakes to the core basin, then McClellan Ridge past the Prong
current.descent: This route's crux move is on the ridge itself, not a technical descent: from the ridge crest (reached via the ascent line west of the Prong), drop roughly 70 vertical feet off the crest and wrap around to the south side of McClellan Peak, then scramble up class 3 rock to the true summit. Descend by reversing this exact sequence: downclimb the class 3 south-side rock back to the ~70-ft notch below the ridge crest, regain the crest, and drop back down the steep talus/scree/snow slope west of the Prong to the flat area between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes at ~7,000 ft. From there, rejoin the Snow Lakes Trail (No. 1553) and retrace it past Lake Viviane, the Snow Lakes, and Nada Lake back to the trailhead — summit-to-trailhead typically takes roughly 5–5.5 hours. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required. Watch for loose rock and exposure on the class 3 downclimb (parties have noted going down 20 ft and wrapping to an easier gully when the direct line felt too exposed), ice on the ridge slope in late season, and the same logjam crossing between the Snow Lakes on the way out. Carry an axe/microspikes if snow lingers on the upper slope, since a slip there has real runout consequences.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the easiest line; movement is unroped scrambling. The demands are navigation and stamina across a broad mountain rather than any gear.

name: Summit Block Scramble (from Stehekin)
beta: From High Bridge the trail passes Howard Lake, climbs a long, hot, dusty switchback up an open southwestern shoulder, then drops into subalpine fir/pine forest and crosses a clear creek before reaching the lower of two glacial cirques on a rocky, sandy moraine. Heaton Camp (~6,700 ft), the only established camp, sits just above the terminal moraine. Another set of switchbacks above camp ends in about a third of a mile at a rocky outcropping, where the maintained trail stops. From there a talus slope leads to the base of the summit; the scramble is 'not particularly technical' but steep, with loose footing and real exposure in places, marked by faint red paint arrows, and crosses a snowfield above the Sandalee Glacier before reaching the old fire-lookout site and the radio tower at the true summit.
overview: McGregor Mountain is the highest and most prominent summit overlooking the Stehekin Valley, gaining over a vertical mile from the valley floor above Lake Chelan. The standard route follows the McGregor Mountain Trail from High Bridge past Howard Lake (historically Coon Lake) to Heaton Camp at about 6,700 ft, then continues about 0.5 mile to a large talus slope below the summit block. A former fire lookout stood on the true summit until it was removed in the 1950s; a radio repeater now marks the top and serves as a landmark. The final pitch is a Class 3 hand-and-foot scramble up talus and along exposed rocky ledges, way-marked by faded, intermittent red arrows and cairns painted years ago — route-finding is the real crux, not the climbing difficulty.

current.approach: McGregor Mountain is only reachable via Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan, which has no outside road access — get there by the Lady of the Lake ferry, floatplane, or the long trail from Cascade Pass/Bridge Creek. From Stehekin Landing, take the NPS shuttle bus (or walk/bike) 11 miles up the Stehekin Valley Road to its end at High Bridge (a hiking permit is required for the overnight version of this trip). From High Bridge, follow the Old Wagon Road/PCT north to Howard Lake at about 1.3 miles; the signed junction where the McGregor Mountain Trail forks right is just beyond the lake — Howard Lake is a reliable water source and a good gut-check that you're on route. Beyond the lake the trail switchbacks relentlessly (climbers report close to 100 switchbacks) up through forest and rocky slopes that get hot and dry with little shade or water, gaining well over 5,000 ft over the next 5.5-6 miles to Heaton Camp at about 6,700 ft, a small single-party designated site where a seasonal-snowmelt stream just below camp is the last dependable water before the summit push. From Heaton Camp the maintained trail continues another quarter- to half-mile to where it ends at the base of a talus field; total stats to the true summit are about 7.75 miles and 6,600 ft one-way. The final roughly 1,000-1,100 vertical feet is an exposed Class 2-3 scramble, not a trail: intermittent (and often faded) red arrows painted on the rock mark the line, which loops right then left behind a lower sub-summit, crosses a snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier, then follows a fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation to the true summit and former fire-lookout site. Carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the shelf above the glacier (common into midsummer), and expect loose rock ('kitty litter' on slabs) and real exposure on the ledges near the top — staying precisely on the arrow-marked line matters, as it gets noticeably dicier off-route.
approach_variant_names: High Bridge and the McGregor Mountain Trail
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route. Reverse the scramble exactly: downclimb the ledgy, loose upper 1,000-1,100 ft back along the red-arrow line past the Sandalee Glacier snowfield/talus shelf and around the lower sub-summit to the top of the main talus field below Heaton Camp. Multiple trip reports specifically flag the descent as the more dangerous half of the trip — loose, gravelly ('kitty litter') slab sections sit right above significant exposure, so downclimb deliberately, stay right on the marked route, and consider a helmet for the scramble portion. Once back on maintained trail at Heaton Camp, it's a long reversal of the approach: roughly 6-7 miles and nearly 100 switchbacks back down past Howard Lake to High Bridge, then the shuttle road (or shuttle bus, if timed right) back to Stehekin Landing. If early-season snow still covers the upper talus/glacier shelf, some parties glissade short, low-angle snow sections with an ice axe for self-arrest rather than downclimbing rock, but there is no fixed rappel infrastructure on this route.
rack: Short handline: 2 shoulder-length slings + 1 double-length sling for exposed sections (optional, for confidence)
bivy: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
current.rope_note: The final summit scramble above the maintained Stehekin-side trail climbs loose Class 3 rock marked by faded red/orange arrows, passing through a notch left of the summit. Parties describe serious exposure in several places — a short handline is prudent for less-experienced parties, though most scramblers go unroped.

name: Southwest Ridge
beta: Parties reach the east end of the Terror Glacier via the same Terror Basin approach as the West Ridge, then climb roughly six pitches of alpine rock (up to 5.8-, rated PG13) up the southwest ridge/face to the summit. There is no pitch-by-pitch description; most parties climb it fully roped rather than scrambled.
overview: A sustained six-pitch 5.8- alpine rock line up West McMillan Spire's southwest ridge, harder and more technical than the standard West Ridge scramble but sharing the same long approach via Terror Basin and the Terror Glacier.

current.approach: Identical to the West Ridge approach: Goodell Creek trailhead to Terror Basin over the 6,200' notch, then traverse benches/slabs to the glacial lake outlet and up slabs onto the Terror Glacier. From there, continue to the east end of the Terror Glacier to reach the base of the southwest ridge (rather than the west-ridge gully used by the standard route).
approach_variant_names: As for the West Ridge to the Terror Glacier, then all the way to the glacier's east end
current.descent: From the summit, descend via the West Ridge's 3rd-4th class scramble and snow/ice gully back onto the Terror Glacier (rather than rappelling the southwest ridge), then re-cross the glacier and slabs to the lake outlet and climb back out over the 6,200' notch to the Goodell Creek trail.
current.detailed_rack: A medium alpine rock rack — small-to-mid cams and a set of nuts — plus 8-10 shoulder-length runners for the long, wandering pitches.
rack: 1 snow picket + ice axe for approach
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine rock protection to about 2-3 inches with 8-10 runners to manage rope drag on the long, wandering pitches. The crux final pitch (5.8- PG13) protects only moderately well. Helmet and a single ice axe for the shared glacier approach.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
current.rope_note: Confirmed: West McMillan Spire, Southwest Ridge, Trad with Steep Snow, 5.8-, 2-star classic (distinct from the easier 4th-class West Ridge on the same peak). Approach through Terror Basin and across the Terror Glacier crosses glaciated/steep snow terrain requiring ice axe and crampons.

name: West Ridge / Southwest Approach
beta: From a high camp in Terror Basin, cross rocky benches and the Terror Glacier's outlet lake, then climb onto the glacier and pick a line to the base of the ridge. A steep snow/ice gully (steepening to roughly 40 degrees near the top) leads to the ~7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire. From the col, follow the west ridge over broken rock, heather, scree and talus — climbers can choose more solid rock steps or looser talus depending on preference — to a short, exposed class 3-4 move onto the summit block.
overview: West McMillan Spire is the taller of the twin McMillan Spires and, by Southern Picket standards, a relatively attainable summit — most parties treat it as their introduction to the range. The technical climbing itself is moderate (a snow gully to a 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire, then class 3-4 ridge scrambling with one short, exposed step below the true summit), but the approach is the real crux: an overgrown, log-choked trail up Goodell Creek, an unofficial steep climber's trail onto a forested ridge, and a rising traverse into Terror Basin before the peak is even in reach. First climbed via this line in 1940 by Fred and Helmy Beckey.

current.approach: From the Goodell Creek (Upper Group Campground) trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers'-path (no trail number — this is a boot path, not a maintained Park trail) that starts behind a large boulder near the campground. There is reliable running water along the roadbed and at a stream crossing just before the steep climb begins, then none reliable again until Terror Basin, so top off bottles there. The path first follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed up the valley for about 4 miles at a gentle grade and is notorious for blowdown — expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs. At a cairned turnoff near 1,700 ft it turns uphill and switchbacks through forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek; around 3,200 ft it gains the crest of the forested ridge, and the whole climb from the turnoff is a steady, unrelenting 4,000 ft of gain in about 2 miles. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, and makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft before kicking up a final steep gully. From there, heather benches and open slabs lead north for a couple of miles, with blueberries in late summer, to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft — the high point of the approach. The north side of this notch is the crux of the approach, not the climb: in late-season/low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet (stay skier's-right — going straight down is a bad idea); early in the season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short, steeper headwall (reported up to ~80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft) that some parties rope up for or protect with a short lower. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp. From camp, a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, reaches a glacial lake outlet and then slabs below the Terror Glacier remnant; the glacier crossing is short and low-angle but can show bare ice by late summer — most parties cross unroped in stable conditions with crampons on. This leads to the base of the snow/rock gully that climbs to the 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire, where the technical climbing begins. One-way distance from car to high camp is roughly 7-8 miles with 6,000+ ft of gain; a fit, loaded party should plan on 6-8+ hours.
approach_variant_names: Goodell Creek climbers' path to the 6,200 ft notch and Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier to the Inspiration-McMillan col gully
current.descent: This route is descended by reversing the line of ascent essentially top to bottom — there is no separate walk-off. From the summit, downclimb the short, exposed Class 3 rock back down to the base of the summit block, then reverse the scree-and-heather ridge to the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col and descend the snow/rock gully below it, following the same snow finger climbed on the way up.
