That finger is glissade-able in soft, sun-affected afternoon snow, but if it is firm or icy (common in the morning or early season) parties often belay the downclimb or make a single short rappel/lower instead — one rope length is plenty (a single 30m section has been reported as sufficient), off natural anchors since there is nothing bolted or fixed on this route: a sling around a rock horn on the rock steps near the col, or a snow bollard/picket if the finger itself is icy. From the foot of the gully, recross the Terror Glacier remnant and the granite benches back toward Terror Basin, then climb back up the loose, chossy north-side gully to the ridge notch (the same skier's-right line used on the approach — avoid the direct fall line) and descend the heather benches on its far side toward the Goodell Creek drainage. From there it's a straightforward but long retrace of the forested trail, roughly 4 miles through the blowdown-choked lower section, back to the Goodell Creek trailhead. Total descent is on the order of 8,000-10,000 ft of elevation loss. The one rappel/protected-lower point is condition-dependent — more likely needed early season or in icy conditions on the snow finger or notch headwall — rather than a fixed technical rappel every party makes.
current.detailed_rack: A technical rack is optional rather than mandatory. Some parties bring a light rope and a small rack of cams/nuts to protect the short exposed class 3-4 step below the summit block, but many climb the entire route unroped.
current.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed overall — a light rack of a few slings/small cams or nuts covers the short, exposed class 3-4 step near the summit; the rope is mostly for security and an optional short rappel rather than sustained pitched climbing.

name: Mile High Club
beta: Excellent, solid rock, an outstanding summit position, and a quick, easy approach/descent have made this the area's most-climbed line (250+ logged ascents). Fully bolted — a rack of quickdraws and a rope is all that's needed. Grades run 5.8-5.10a across 7 pitches on the crest of the pillar.
overview: Mile High Club is a striking, fully-bolted 7-pitch alpine sport route (700 ft, Grade III, 5.10a) up the southwest arête of Eros Tower (aka Vega North Tower), a rock sub-summit just north of Morning Star Peak's true 6,020 ft summit — this route does not reach the main summit. First climbed by Darin Berdinka and Rad Roberts, it's regarded as one of the best moderate multi-pitch outings in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor: solid rock, sustained 5.9-5.10a climbing, and an airy, exposed finish.

current.approach: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065). Follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) north; the first mile crosses two significant creeks with no bridges (a log crossing, a root crossing, and one more insistent ford), so expect wet feet and use caution in early season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest and, after roughly 2.5 miles and about 1,950 ft of gain, reaches the last major switchback (~4,300 ft) just before the tread begins zig-zagging steeply up toward Headlee Pass. Leave the maintained trail here and traverse northeast on a surprisingly easy, cairned line across a talus field toward the Mile High buttress (the striking pillar also called Eros Tower / Vega North Tower, a 5,280 ft sub-summit north of Morning Star's main summit). Route-finding landmarks: pass just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through the trees into a second open talus field, cross open heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff, then ascend to the obvious red gully to the right of the buttress. A convenient seep just below the Mile High gully is the only reliable water on the approach, and only runs through mid-season. From the gully, scramble up and left on rubble-strewn, loose ledges (careful footing/rockfall management for parties below) to a lone fir tree, then follow a narrow ledge about 20 ft to a single bolted belay marking the start of Pitch 1. Plan roughly 1–1.5 hours from the trailhead to the base once you know the line; it is unmarked past the switchback and has caught out parties who don't have beta or GPS coordinates for the turnoff.
approach_variant_names: Sunrise Mine Trail to the cairned talus traverse
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7; rap 2 face-rappels to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 70m rope is sufficient for all 8 raps; two 60m ropes also work if you'd rather split gear or prefer doubled-rope security, and some parties carry a single 60m instead but report tighter/more numerous transitions. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted sport-alpine route — no cams or nuts required. Carry about a dozen quickdraws plus 2-3 alpine draws for drag management, and a single 60m rope (sufficient for all 8 raps) or two 60m/one 70m rope for faster double-rope rappels.
current.pro_needs: Bolts only; a dozen quickdraws covers all 7 pitches.
current.rope_note: 700ft, III 5.10a, 7 pitches on the Mile High buttress. Fully bolted face climbing; rappel the route on a single 60m or two 60s.

name: Miracle Ramps
beta: Climbs a horizontal crack, hogback ridges and diagonal cracks to a smeary crux at four bolts (the route's namesake 'miracle' section), then continues through knobby slab, an undercling ('Ruffled Crack'), overlap climbing and flake systems to a summit anchor.
overview: A 6-pitch variation of the first six pitches of the older Primal Scream, up the right side of a central buttress on the South Face, finishing at its own summit anchor.

current.approach: From the grassy saddle bivy, ascend class 4 ramps to a dihedral, then to the starting wall ledge shared with Primal Scream.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: 6 rappels down the route via two-bolt stainless in-line chain anchors.
current.detailed_rack: Standard single rack to 3"; anchors are two-bolt stainless in-line chain anchors at every belay.
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolt-protected slab/knob climbing with gear backup on the crack and flake sections (pitches 1, 3, 6).

name: East Face / East Buttress
beta: From Cascade Pass, contour south up Mixup Arm and across a roughly 6,000 ft bench to a small glacier/snowfield below Gunsight Notch; rope up to cross it. From the notch's south side, two roped pitches (a loose gully, then a short chimney/scramble) gain a shoulder below the main summit pyramid. From there, easy class 3-4 scrambling up the light-gray 'white staircase' leads to a short mid-5th-class step through a notch in the exposed summit ridge, then a short class 3-4 ridge walk to the true summit. Descend the same line via 5 rappels.
overview: Mix-up Peak (7,440 ft) sits one mile south of Cascade Pass on the Skagit–Chelan county line and marks the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. First climbed in 1947 by Wesley Grande and Jack Kendrick, its East Face is a compact, mostly solid-rock 'staircase' of class 3–4 scrambling with a short mid-5th-class step near the top, reached by a glacier/snowfield crossing from Cascade Pass. It's a popular objective (7-9 hours from the trailhead to the summit alone) for parties already in the Cascade Pass basin, but the approach's moat and rockfall-prone notches keep it a genuine alpine outing despite the modest elevation.

current.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15), elevation ~3,600 ft. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail (a well-graded, switchbacking National Park trail, unnumbered but universally called the Cascade Pass Trail) 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — a broad, scenic saddle with no reliable water beyond seasonal snowmelt, so top off at a creek crossing lower on the trail. From the pass, do not continue on the maintained Pacific Crest/Stehekin trail; instead pick up a climbers' path on the right (south) side that bends SSE and makes a rising traverse across the heather-and-talus flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour. This traverse crosses a minor spur ridge and several steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer — in early season these have poor runout above a roughly 400 ft drop, so an ice axe and comfort with a traverse on firm snow are important; a slip here has real consequences. Continue traversing to the toe of the Cache Glacier (~6,000-6,200 ft), then ascend moderate glaciated/snow slopes (watch for crevasses in early-mid season) aiming for the obvious notch system below and left of Mixup's summit — commonly called the 'V-notch' — just north of Gunsight Notch, the main portal between Mixup, the Triplets, and Cascade Peak. Gain the notch/saddle via a short snow or scree gully, then work up class 3-4 ramps on the east side to a feature climbers call the 'White Staircase' (exposed class 3), which leads to a point roughly 100 ft below the summit where the roped mid-5th-class pitches of the East Face/East Buttress begin. Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass itself and on Mixup Arm, so parties either push the whole approach and climb as one very long car-to-car day (7-9 hours to the summit alone), or continue past the notch/Cache Col area to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (~6,120 ft) or near Cache Col for a lower-effort summit day. Rockfall — both natural and climber-triggered — is a real hazard on the upper approach gullies and staircase; keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm bench and the Cache Glacier
current.descent: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, from the bottom of the shoulder, one rappel on a single 60 m rope reaches the belay station at the top of the second climbing pitch. From there the line drops over an overhanging section to just below the north side of Gunsight Notch: one double-rope rappel with two ropes, or two rappels on a single 60 m rope. That is four rappels on one 60 m rope, which is what parties report, or three with two ropes. Anchors are fixed natural slings and cord rather than bolts, and parties regularly add cord or rebuild one, so carry some. Move off the fall line as soon as you are down each rappel; rockfall knocked loose by the party above is a recognized hazard here. Below the notch, re-descend the glacier and snowfield and Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass.
current.detailed_rack: A light selection of cams and nuts up to 2 inches handles the brief fifth-class steps.
current.pro_needs: Gear is used sparingly: a light rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts to ~2in) covers the short mid-5th-class step and any anchor-building at the moat/notch. Most of the route is unroped class 3-4 scrambling on solid rock.

name: Mojo Rising
beta: P1 is a bolted face (~105 ft, 11b/A0) with a runout 5.6 section before the first bolt; the 'Skywalker Traverse' features on P4; P5 is ~175 ft at 5.10a with an awkward seam and a 5.9 corner finger crack; final pitches (7-9) ease to 5.4 and are often simul-climbed or pitched out on the well-traveled Southwest Rib.
overview: A direct-start variation to the Northwest Face on SEWS, first climbed III 5.11 A1 (with a short section of aid) by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Tom Smith, October 13-14, 2006; the 5.11b grade covers the free climbing only — the aid section has not been reported freed.

current.approach: Approach as for the Northwest Face: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail ~1-1.25 miles to the NW-side clearing, then the climber's path up talus into the basin below the west face. Mojo Rising starts on an obvious bolted face about 20 ft downhill from a large chockstone-filled chimney/notch feature, just left of pitch 1 of the Northwest Face (Boving-Pollock) route — the chockstone chimney is the key landmark for locating the start among several closely-spaced lines on this wall.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the basin below the west face, then 20 ft downhill of the chockstone chimney
current.descent: Mojo Rising offers two descent options depending on the day's plan. To bail or descend the route itself, rappel the first 3 pitches with a single 60m rope from bolted/chain anchors back to the ground. To finish the full climb, pitches 7-9 are typically simul-climbed or pitched out onto the well-traveled Southwest Rib finish to the true summit; from there, take the standard South Arete descent — downclimb the arete to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base, and hike out via the Blue Lake Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles of small-to-medium cams (roughly BD 0.2-2), offset cams for thin placements, a full set of nuts with extra micro brass stoppers, and at least 11 draws for the bolted sections.
rack: Doubles cams 0.2-2in, offset cams for thin placements
Full nut set + extra micro brass stoppers
current.pro_needs: The aid section has not been freed; strong 5.10+ climbers recommended for the bolted/runout P1.
current.rope_note: 5.11b sport/trad hybrid pitch(es) on SEWS, same buttress as Free Mojo/Northwest Face; mixed protection.

name: Monkey On A Woodpile
beta: Start on the right (east) side of the dike and follow bolts through loose blocks to the anchor. A left-side variation exists with looser rock and minimal 5th-class climbing; the right side is steeper at the stated grade.
overview: Beginner-friendly sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Lower from the anchor (left variation uses quicklinks on hangers; right variation uses fixed shuts).
current.detailed_rack: ~6-7 bolts of uncertain condition to the anchor; bring extra draws given the route's low traffic.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted; inspect bolts/hangers before committing given noted uncertain condition.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: North Col
beta: From Glacier Basin, leave the trail and climb steep snow (up to ~45 degrees) through a gully/cliff-band system to reach the North Col (6,760+ ft). From the col, a short crux chimney (three moves rated 5.6, 5.2, 5.6, now bolted) gains a ledge system; a rap anchor sits about 25 ft above the start of the chimney. From there a steepish ramp leads left for roughly 100 ft (snow whales can slicken it), after which the route becomes class 3 scrambling, with some avoidable class 4, on loose volcanic breccia to the summit — the final ~200 ft is reported as the worst rock on the route.
overview: Monte Cristo Peak (7,136 ft) is the technical centerpiece of the Monte Cristo Group, a tight cluster of peaks (Kyes, Cadet, Columbia, Del Campo) ringing the ghost town of Monte Cristo in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. Unlike its neighbors, Monte Cristo has no scramble-only line to the true summit: the standard and most-climbed route, the North Col Route, requires roped 5.6 rock climbing through a short chimney above the col, so it's properly a Basic Alpine Climb rather than a Class 3 scramble. The peak was first climbed in 1923 by James M. Keyes and W. Zerum, and in 1918 it was described as a huge mass of red rock.

current.approach: From the Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of the paved Mountain Loop Highway drive), the approach is in two clearly different stages before you ever leave a maintained tread. Stage one is 4 flat, easy miles up the gated, washed-out Monte Cristo Road along the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo ghost town (~2,800 ft) — a couple of cable/suspension bridges cross the river en route, and this stretch is runnable/bikeable in dry conditions. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek, and follow "Dumas Street" through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. Stage two is the real climb: the first half-mile follows an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek, then the trail turns into slick rock scrambling more than hiking — steep, eroded, hands-on-rock terrain climbing past Glacier Falls, with numerous cascades and slick, root-braided rock steps that are notably harder (and slicker) descending than ascending. The trail crosses into Henry M. Jackson Wilderness and skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill before leveling out into Glacier Basin (~4,500 ft) after about 2.5 miles and ~1,700 ft of gain from Monte Cristo — roughly 6.5 miles and ~2,100 ft from the car. Glacier Creek parallels the whole climb and is a reliable water source, but it drains historic mine workings — treat/filter and be aware of elevated arsenic/heavy-metal readings noted by the Forest Service, especially in the lower reaches near the old townsite. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb open talus and (typically) persistent steep snow — up to ~45° for a few hundred vertical feet — directly toward the obvious North Col (~6,760+ ft) on Monte Cristo's north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks and Wilmans Glacier looming close overhead to climber's right. An ice axe and comfort on steep firm snow are essentially mandatory into midsummer; a moat can open at the col and the step across it can be intimidating or, late season, impassable. From the North Col, contour south (skier's/climber's left) across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting for the obvious break/gully in the rock that gives the easiest way up to the base of the short summit chimney.
approach_variant_names: Barlow Pass, the closed road and Glacier Basin
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line (the North Col Route is a there-and-back, not a loop). From the summit, downclimb the ~100 ft of Class 3 terrain back to the top of the short chimney. The chimney itself is the technical crux both ways — about 30 ft requiring three moves of exposed climbing (roughly 5.6, 5.2, 5.6) — and most parties rappel it rather than downclimb, especially with a second climber or in the wet/mossy conditions common on this shaded north-facing rock. A fixed/bolted rappel anchor (reported as a single new-ish bolt backed up by a natural nut placement) sits a short distance below the chimney; a single 60m rope is sufficient to reach easier ground. Treat the bolt+nut anchor with normal backcountry skepticism — inspect it, and carry a nut or small cam to supplement or replace it if it looks worn, since this is a lightly-traveled scramble route without the anchor redundancy of a popular sport crag. Below the rappel, continue down and contour north back to the North Col, re-cross the moat/schrund, and descend the steep snow slope (glissade only if you can self-arrest reliably; it firms up fast in the afternoon shade) back down to the talus and into Glacier Basin. From there it's a plain hike out: reverse Trail #719 down through the slick-rock section above Glacier Falls (use extra caution here — this is the section trip reports flag as harder and more slip-prone descending than climbing), back through Monte Cristo townsite, and out the 4 miles of old road to Barlow Pass. Helmets are recommended for the entire upper mountain (col to summit) given loose rock in the chimney/gully and any parties above.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack suffices: a 60m rope and a handful of small-to-medium stoppers and slings for the ~30 ft bolted 5.6 chimney. A single rappel off the bolted anchor descends the chimney.
rack: 60m rope for the roped chimney section and its rappel (three moves: 5.6, 5.2, 5.6)
A few small cams/nuts, optional, as backup to reported (unconfirmed) bolts
2-3 slings for a gully belay/rappel anchor
current.pro_needs: A few small-to-medium cams and/or slings for the ~30-75 ft chimney (reported as three roped moves: 5.6, 5.2, 5.6); a 60m rope covers the technical section and its rappel. Fixed bolts have been reported in recent years but should not be solely relied upon.
bivy: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
current.rope_note: North Col standard route: steep talus/snow to the North Col, then a ~75ft gully (a belay may be needed crossing the moat/steep step) with Class 2-3 ledges near the top. Descent retraces the route; one ~75ft rappel may be necessary.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From a high camp near Lake of the Woods or in the Monument-Lake / Lower Monument basin, gain Monument's south ridge crest (~6,900 ft) via a left-angling ramp system, then follow the broad ridge northwest for over a mile on class 2 talus. A false summit near 8,000 ft requires a short, light class 3 scramble; from there one or two more class 3 moves lead to the true 8,597 ft summit, which features a distinctive leaning summit horn. The peak can also be approached from basins on its east/northeast side via the Monument Creek Trail, or from the north via Shellrock Pass.
overview: Monument Peak is the most rugged and inaccessible peak in the Lago group, deep in the eastern Pasayten Wilderness near the Eureka Creek country. Double-nubbed and built of granite, it sits almost as an island: Eureka Creek wraps its north, west, and south sides while Monument Creek drains the east side. The mountain has a precipitous north/northeast side, a cliffy east face, a rugged west face, and a comparatively gentler (though still remote) south slope that forms the standard scramble line. A disheveled connecting ridge links it to 8,397-ft Blackcap Mountain a half-mile north; 8,745-ft Mount Lago, its line parent, lies about 2.4 miles further north. First ascended in 1978 by Fred Beckey and John Roper.

current.approach: Four approaches reach Monument Peak, all long and remote — this is deep in the Pasayten Wilderness near the Canadian border, and most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a high camp. The most common is via the Monument Creek Trailhead on Lost River Road/FR 5400 (about 22 miles northwest of Winthrop via Mazama), starting at roughly 2,400 ft. From the trailhead, follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley; the first ~4 miles are well-maintained through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the Eureka Creek confluence (Eureka Falls Camp) — this is your last easy, reliable water before a long dry stretch. Beyond Eureka Creek the trail has been essentially unmaintained for 25+ years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Ford Eureka Creek (can run thigh-to-waist deep during snowmelt — a genuine early-summer hazard) then pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge, following it up to 7,100-ft Pistol Pass around mile 11. From the pass, descend about a mile on the trail, finishing on a short spur, to Lake of the Woods in the Monument–Lake Mountain basin, a common high camp — about 12 miles and 5,300 ft of gain from the trailhead. From camp, traverse cross-country northwest to the ~7,400-ft saddle below Lake Mountain, then descend into Lower Monument Basin (~6,100 ft); the lake-outlet creek here is your last dependable water for the summit push and can shrink to a trickle late in the season. From the basin, climb a left-angling ramp system to gain Monument Peak's south/southeast ridge at about 6,900 ft, then follow a long talus traverse toward the summit. The final section involves roughly a half-pitch of Class 3 (locally Class 3-4) scrambling where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes, sometimes complicated by a steep snowfield just below the true summit that can still require an ice axe (or a class 3/4 rock detour around its left side) into midsummer. Three alternative approaches exist: dropping in from 6,960-ft Slate Pass on the Harts Pass Road down to the Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 and Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A (reportedly the easiest, though not shortest, reaching the same basin from the north); via the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead just past Harts Pass on Trail No. 498, crossing the Middle Fork Pasayten River and picking up Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 then Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A; or a longer approach from the Lost Creek/Monument Creek trailhead side. Whichever line is used, expect long, remote travel with significant off-trail brush and route-finding on the final miles — carry a map/GPS and budget extra time.
approach_variant_names: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail
current.descent: This is a walk-off — there is no rappelling on the standard scramble route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 3 (occasionally 3-4) rock/talus off the summit block to regain the south/southeast ridge at roughly 6,900 ft, then descend the left-angling ramp system back into Lower Monument Basin, topping off water at the lake-outlet creek if needed, before climbing back up to the Lake Mountain saddle (~7,400 ft) and dropping to high camp at Lake of the Woods. Where a summit snowfield was crossed on the ascent, most parties recross it on foot (or skirt around its left side on rock) rather than glissade, since it can remain firm or icy well into summer. The main descent hazards are loose talus, exposed Class 3 scrambling near the summit, and route-finding fatigue — several parties describe finishing the final talus slopes back to camp by headlamp. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel gear are used on this route. From camp, retrace whichever approach trail was used — Pistol Pass and the Eureka Creek ford back to the Monument Creek Trailhead, or the Ferguson Lake/Robinson Creek trail back to Slate Pass or the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead — to reach the road.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
current.rope_note: Remote Pasayten scramble via Pistol Pass/Lake of the Woods approach: left-angling ramp to the south ridge, then long talus slopes with Class 3 scrambling. No rope or fixed protection mentioned in any trip report; the crux is remoteness/route-finding and water availability, not technical terrain.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: The Standard Scramble represents the basic approach to Morning Star Peak's 6,020 ft summit. Multiple scramble options exist on the peak, including the South Ridge and Northwest Face routes, both of which involve Class 3 scrambling with sections of steep rock and snow.
overview: Morning Star Peak (6,020 ft) sits above Headlee Pass and the Sunrise Mine basin between Sperry and Del Campo Peaks, in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District). The standard route leaves the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile in, before the South Fork Stillaguamish crossing, and climbs the brushy river valley and snow-covered slabs to a notch in the southeast ridge, then a steep gully to the south ridge and the summit. The South Ridge scramble requires comfort on steep rock and snow and is tougher than the Class 2-3 label alone suggests, especially in early season. Route-finding takes some care, and the snow-covered slabs below the notch are the route's main avalanche concern.

current.approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) about half a mile. Just before the trail crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish River, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side, or take the line of least resistance along that side. The path soon fades into slide alder, brush and rock debris; fording the river to dodge the brush is hazardous in high runoff, especially in late spring and early summer. Work up the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,100 ft, then either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin (about 4,000 ft), or continue to a broad basin at about 3,700 ft and climb the steep gully (or the slabs to its right) directly east of it, leaving it to the right where that is easy. Climb snow-covered slabs to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft; these slabs are the route's main avalanche concern. The round trip is roughly 5.5-6 miles with 3,700-4,200 ft of gain. The steep gully is often icy when snow-filled, so helmet, ice axe and crampons are standard early in the season; early-season snow makes this a basic alpine climb rather than a scramble.
approach_variant_names: South Fork Stillaguamish valley
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent line, there is no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels). From the 6,020 ft summit, descend on or near the south ridge to the broad gully, downclimb it into the southeast basin, traverse back below the cliffs and climb about 200 ft through trees to the notch in the southeast ridge. The gully (icy in early/mid-season) is often easier to face in and downclimb than to descend facing out, and crampons make the icy sections much smoother; groups should stay tight and avoid stacking directly above one another. From the notch, descend the snow-covered slabs (watch for avalanche conditions) and the gully or ridge ramp back into the South Fork Stillaguamish valley, then retrace the brushy east-side path to the Sunrise Mine Trail and the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack.
current.pro_needs: None.
bivy: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass

name: Moss Out For Harambe
beta: Follows an open book formation through moss and ferns. Climbers pull a feature nicknamed 'Harambe's nose' to reach a block above and right of a monkey-face visible in the rock, then proceed under a roof overhang (placing gear), traverse left into an 'awesome lieback flake' — the 5.7 crux — and finish up easier slab. The route is named for the monkey-face feature in the wall.
overview: A one-pitch 5.7 trad line up Mossy Loaf's upper tier, climbing an open-book past a distinctive 'monkey face' rock feature to a roof, then a steep lieback flake crux before easing off on slab.

current.approach: From the Barlow Pass gate, walk the closed road (old railroad grade) approximately 4 miles to the Monte Cristo townsite; a backcountry campground sits at that mark. Mossy Loaf's coordinates place it essentially at/immediately adjacent to the townsite itself, so once at the flat of Monte Cristo the formation is only a short distance further off the main townsite path. The exact final spur to the specific wall is not well established, so on-site scouting is recommended for the last stretch.
current.descent: From the top of the route, downclimb the easy slab above the crux or scramble off along the wall's edge back to road level. The standard walk-off between tiers involves some bushwhacking, which is one reason the neighboring route You Moss Be Joking exists as a lower-impact link.
current.detailed_rack: Standard trad rack to 5 inches; a single Black Diamond #4 cam is useful near the top and could allow running out the final easier ground.
current.pro_needs: Gear to 5 inches; solid finger-to-hand-size placements protect the lieback-flake crux and the roof traverse best.
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta could be found for 'Mossy Loaf' or this route under any name. Gear inferred from the 5.7 alpine grade and the crag's 'mossy' naming convention, comparable to other low-to-mid 5th class, lichen/moss-covered Cascades alpine rock.

name: Lava Glacier Headwall
beta: The headwall forms a triangle between the North Ridge and the Lava Ridge and is climbed as moderate-to-steep glacier ice/snow up through the triangle to gain the upper mountain. It qualifies for the Mazamas' '16 Major NW Peaks' and 'Guardian Peaks' award routes and is typically done car-to-car in two or more days.
overview: A steep snow/ice headwall filling the triangle between the North Ridge and Lava Ridge, above the Lava Glacier. The historic line crosses the lowest of three bergschrunds on the glacier's west side beneath the North Ridge, then climbs diagonally up the headwall using rock outcrops for protection from near-continuous rockfall; a documented variant follows an obvious chute at mid-height. Like Adams' other headwall routes, it sees few repeats and should only be attempted early season in cold, stable conditions.

current.approach: Same trailhead and trail as the Lyman Glacier approach: Killen Creek Trail #113 from the Killen Creek Trailhead, about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest (crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5) to the PCT at ~6,100 ft, then the High Camp Trail #10 another 1.0 mile to High Camp/Adams Glacier Meadows (~6,900 ft). From High Camp, the Lava Glacier Headwall is reached more directly than Lyman: traverse off-trail across the lava fields toward the toe of the Lava Glacier without needing to work around Lava Ridge, reaching the base of the headwall (the triangular ice/snow face bounded by the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other). This is glacial/talus terrain with crevasse hazard on the glacier itself. Sources consistently stress climbing this face early season — late spring to early summer — since it becomes icy and rockfall-prone as the snowpack recedes later in summer.
approach_variant_names: Killen Creek, the PCT and High Camp, then across the lava fields to the Lava Glacier
current.descent: Descend the North Ridge back toward High Camp, the same non-technical but tedious scree/boulder walk-off used for the Adams Glacier and Lyman Glacier routes on this side of the mountain — long, loose volcanic scree, some narrow/exposed sections, and rockfall risk onto other parties, but no rappelling required on the standard line. From High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. The alternative is to continue over the summit and descend the South Climb route to Cold Springs, which lands you at a different trailhead and requires a shuttle.
current.detailed_rack: Snow anchors (pickets); occasional ice screw for firmer or icy sections.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall
current.rope_note: Two ice tools, ice screws and a couple of pickets, crampons and a helmet, plus a glacier rope and crevasse rescue kit for the Lava Glacier below. Expect to move continuously rather than pitch the headwall out: it is around 45-degree neve, and the reason not to stop is rockfall rather than difficulty. Nothing on the route is rappelled - the way off walks down the North Ridge - so the rope is there for the glacier and the bergschrund at the base. Go early season; later the headwall turns icy and starts shedding rock.

name: Mazama Glacier Headwall
beta: An easy glacier climb with long stretches of steep glacier travel and an optional short technical pitch at the very top. From Sunrise Camp, ascend a 40° glacier, then veer right up a 45° headwall to a narrowing strip of glacier leading to Piker's Peak; climbers may exit left on a 25-30° field or continue right through an optional 60-70° snow/ice section.
overview: A big, scenic, mostly non-technical glacier climb up the east side of Mount Adams from Bird Creek Meadows, with an optional short technical pitch near the top.

current.approach: Start from the Bird Creek Road trailhead (~5,700 ft) on the Yakama Reservation side; route-finding across moraines and glacier fields begins around 6,700 ft, reaching Sunrise Camp at 8,300 ft. The Yakama Nation decides each year whether overnight stays are allowed, so plan a single-day push in day-use-only years.
approach_variant_names: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain trail
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier past Sunrise Camp and out the way you came in to Bird Creek Meadows. Descending the South Spur instead is possible, but it is not a variation on the same day out - it finishes at the Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead on the mountain's south side, reached by an entirely different road system from the Yakama Nation approach this route starts on, so it only works if you have a vehicle waiting there. A party that walks off south without one has left its car on the far side of the mountain.
current.detailed_rack: 2-3 pickets for the 45° headwall; 2-3 ice screws if opting for the steeper technical finish.
current.pro_needs: Optional pickets on the headwall and screws only if taking the steep technical variation at the very top.

name: North Ridge
beta: From high camp near the Adams Glacier moraine, gain the North Ridge (North Cleaver) and follow it upward, bypassing most obstacles on either side, to the summit ice cap; traverse roughly a mile across the plateau to reach the true summit.
overview: Also called the North Cleaver, the North Ridge is Adams' second most-popular summit route and a scenic, less-crowded alternative to the South Climb. It climbs the rock-and-snow rib between the Adams and Lava Glaciers, reached via the quiet Killen Creek approach on the north side, and is most pleasant early season while still largely snow-covered.

current.approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes. A common early start is to camp the night before on the Killen Creek Trail near 6,050 ft, just before the Pacific Crest Trail junction, then leave around 4 am and pass High Camp in the dark.
approach_variant_names: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
current.descent: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. Some parties instead carry over and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs, which requires a long car shuttle. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent. On the way down in early July, staying on the crest line, which cairns mark, is easier than dropping onto the side snow.
current.detailed_rack: Per team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit for the summit ice cap.
current.pro_needs: Snow protection (pickets) for the steeper upper ridge plus glacier-travel gear for the summit ice cap; generally no rock pro.

name: North Ridge (West Face)
beta: A straightforward snow/ice route up to 50°, following the northwest face of the North Ridge. Bring a snow picket, an ice screw, possibly a few thin pins, and two ice tools.
overview: A straightforward snow/ice line up the west face of Mount Adams's North Ridge, a more technical companion route to the standard North Ridge scramble.

current.approach: Start at the Killen Creek trailhead on FR 2329 north of Takhlakh Lake and follow Killen Creek Trail 113 south for about 3.2 miles through lodgepole forest and meadows to the Pacific Crest Trail junction near 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail, a rocky boot path that climbs a volcanic spur for about a mile to High Camp on a flat bench near 6,900 ft; the whole carry is roughly four miles and 2,300 ft. Camp here, since water comes only from snowmelt and the site is very exposed to wind. Above camp the trail ends and the way crosses moraines and old lava flows toward the north side of the mountain, so carry navigation for whiteouts. A Cascade Volcano Pass is required above 7,000 ft.
current.descent: Descend the North Ridge, also called the North Cleaver, back toward High Camp. This is a walk-off over loose volcanic scree and boulders and is longer than it looks from above, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below, so spread out and move quickly through the worst sections. A rock band on the ridge can be downclimbed, and a short rope-assisted step is sometimes used by parties uneasy with the exposure. From High Camp retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail 113 to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A snow picket, at least one ice screw, and a few thin pitons.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rack: picket(s) and a screw or two for the steepest 50° sections.
current.rope_note: Grade II-III on snow and ice up to 50 degrees: a picket, an ice screw and two tools on a 60 m rope. The base is usually inaccessible directly because of a large bergschrund, so parties gain the line off the Adams Glacier and traverse in after crossing crevasses on its west side. Best in June and July - the crevasse route-finding through that traverse gets tricky to impossible later in July.

name: South Climb (South Spur)
beta: The most popular and easiest way up the mountain. From the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead the route follows an old roadbed through the 2012 Cascade Creek burn scar, climbs into subalpine meadows, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then ascends Crescent Ridge to broad snowfields leading past Lunch Counter to Piker's Peak and the true summit. No rope or technical protection is used on the standard line in normal conditions — ice axe and crampons suffice.
overview: Mount Adams's standard, non-technical route: a long snow slog up the broad southern flank via Crescent/Suksdorf Ridge, the Lunch Counter camp, and the false summit ('Piker's Peak') to the true summit beyond a shallow crater traverse.

current.approach: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Rd to the Forest Road 23 junction; bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 junction for South Climb, turn left and follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then follow FR 8040 (steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks — no RVs/trailers) for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead (5,600 ft). The trail follows an old roadbed through the burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadows, crosses Round-the-Mountain Trail #9 and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge to the base of the summit snowfields.
approach_variant_names: Cold Springs trailhead and the Lunch Counter
current.descent: Retrace the ascent line: cross back over the shallow summit crater, down over Piker's Peak, and descend the broad snow slopes of Suksdorf/Crescent Ridge to Lunch Counter, then follow the old roadbed back to the trailhead. Glissading is common on the lower snowfields in firm-but-soft conditions; watch for exposed rock and runout hazards in late season as snow recedes.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard line; rope and glacier gear are not needed.
current.rope_note: Standard/easiest route on Mount Adams — non-technical walk-up via Suksdorf Ridge through Lunch Counter (9,250ft). Ice axe and crampons (or microspikes/trekking poles depending on season) are the essentials; crevasses do not typically appear on this route below the summit. Technical climbing gear is optional.

name: Standard Scramble (Switchback / Klahhane Ridge approach)
beta: From the Switchback Trailhead on Hurricane Ridge Road, hike the Switchback Trail steeply up through subalpine forest (about 700 ft in 0.6 mile) to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge. Turn left and follow that trail roughly half a mile to a broad saddle, where an unsigned climbers' path forks off uphill toward the summit; the maintained trail that climbs on to Victor Pass (5,850 ft) is not the summit route. Take the climbers' path and scramble Class 3 terrain over loose rock/talus to the summit. There is no roped climbing on the standard route, but the exposure and loose rock warrant caution and route-finding care.
overview: Mount Angeles (6,454 ft) is the highest point between Hurricane Ridge and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, rising as a prominent, accessible summit above the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center in the northern Olympics. It's reached by trail almost the whole way, with a short, loose Class 3 scramble guarding the true summit. On a clear day the top gives views across the Strait of Juan de Fuca to Vancouver Island, north to the San Juans, south into the interior Olympics toward Mount Olympus, and (in good visibility) east to Mount Rainier.

current.approach: From the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center parking lot (end of Hurricane Ridge Road, ~17 mi south of Port Angeles via Race St/Hwy 101), start on the paved High Ridge Trail at the east end of the lot. At about 0.3 mi bear toward Sunrise Point/Klahhane Ridge Trail and continue along open, exposed subalpine ridge (alternating meadow and pocket forest) for roughly 2.5 mi to an unsigned junction where a distinct, unmaintained 'climbers trail' splits left (north) off the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail — this is the start of the true scramble route (sometimes mapped as the Mount Angeles Summit Climbers Trail). A shorter, steeper alternative start exists directly off Hurricane Ridge Road at the Switchback Trail (~mile marker in the last few miles before the visitor center), which gains about 700-800 ft in 0.6 mi to meet the Mount Angeles Trail higher up, cutting off some of the ridge walk. From the climbers-trail junction, the primitive use trail climbs steeply through rocky meadows and thinning forest on the peak's west side — this final push is only about 0.6 mi but does roughly 800 of the route's 2,100 total feet of gain (average grade ~27%, max ~42%), topping out around 6,000 ft at the base of the summit block/gully. Route-finding note from on-the-ground reports: don't scramble the first notch you reach — stay on the faint boot path traversing higher to the actual summit gully. From there, most parties scramble the right/east side of the final block, which is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock (the same line the descent explicitly avoids downclimbing) with only brief but exposed final moves to the true summit (6,454 ft). There is no reliable water past the visitor center (which has a seasonal contact station with restrooms/potable water) — carry all you need. Key hazards: lingering rotten/consolidated snow choking the summit notch/gully well into July and August even in normal years, loose scree and fractured, rockfall-prone rock on the upper scramble, and sustained exposure along the open ridge crest.
approach_variant_names: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge
Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills
current.descent: Descend the same way you came up as far as the base of the summit block, but do NOT reverse the ascent gully — parties consistently and strongly recommend downclimbing the left (west) side of the summit block/notch instead, since the direct/right-side ascent line is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock that can trigger rockfall or a slide if downclimbed. This is a class 3 scramble downclimb only; there are no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route, and roped rappelling is not reported as part of the normal descent — a rope is not standard gear here, though a cautious party could choose to hand-line or belay the notch with a single rope and natural gear (a tree/horn sling) if conditions (verglas, wet rock, inexperienced members) warrant it. Below the block, pick back up the primitive climbers trail, drop back to the Klahhane Ridge Trail junction, and retrace the ridge trail (or the Switchback Trail cutoff, if that was your approach) back to the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center — roughly 3.1 mi and 1.5-2 hours from the summit for the average party. Stay alert on the descent specifically at the loose scree below the block and on the exposed notch downclimb: parties often flag descent, not ascent, as the more dangerous part of this route because of accumulated fatigue plus loose rock underfoot.
current.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; the crux is a short exposed Class 3 scramble.
current.rope_note: Standard scramble via Klahhane Ridge or the shorter Switchback Trail (Olympic NP): exposed ridge-walking and a Class 3 rock scramble through loose scree/fractured rock requiring route-finding but no rope or fixed protection. Snow and rotten cornices can linger near the summit into July/August.

name: Lake Ann Approach Scramble
beta: From the Austin Pass/Lake Ann trailhead, hike the maintained Lake Ann Trail, which drops roughly 800 ft into the Swift Creek basin before climbing back out. The summer line follows the crest from the 4,900-ft saddle over Peak 5681; the usual snow-season line differs: near the Lake Ann junction, leave the trail and work up heather benches and talus, staying fairly high on the east side of Mount Annette (nicknamed 'Little Ann') rather than dropping into brush, then continue up a gully (often snow-filled and roughly following a fault line) to gain the summit ridge and the top of Mount Ann. The off-trail portion is generally straightforward Class 2 route-finding, though boot paths can peter out higher up and steeper sections may warrant an ice-axe self-belay. Reported round-trip stats vary by GPS track/route taken (10.5 mi RT / 4,000 ft gain is the commonly listed figure; individual logs have recorded figures as low as ~11 mi / ~3,400 ft), reflecting that this is an off-trail line rather than a fixed path.
overview: Mount Ann is a ~5,840-5,873 ft summit on the ridge dividing Swift Creek from Lake Ann, immediately southwest of Mount Shuksan and roughly a mile outside the North Cascades National Park boundary. It's reached via the heavily-traveled Lake Ann Trail from the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead on the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542): the trail drops into the Swift Creek headwaters basin, climbs past Lake Ann to a 4,900-ft saddle northwest of the lake, then a boot path leaves the maintained trail to follow the ridge crest southwest and south — over an informally-named 'Peak 5681' (called 'Annette' or 'Han' in some trip reports) — before a final ~0.5 mile scramble west along the summit ridge, with close-up views of both the Coleman-Deming side of Mount Baker and the Curtis Glacier/Fisher Chimneys side of Shuksan.

current.approach: From the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead (paved lot at the end of SR 542, roughly 58 miles / 1.5-2 hr from Bellingham), follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600, which drops about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up to a 4,900-ft saddle northwest of Lake Ann, about 3.9 miles one way; the lake itself is a short way farther down the trail. From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest; where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms — follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly 0.5 mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann. Total round trip is about 10.5 miles with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain.
approach_variant_names: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the 4,900 ft saddle, then the boot path and cairns over Peak 5681
current.descent: Descent follows the ascent route in reverse: from the summit ridge, scramble east back over Peak 5681 to the point where the boot path drops off the ridge crest, staying high (rather than contouring low) where the path is indistinct to avoid cliffing out above the basin. Regain the 4,900-ft saddle and rejoin the maintained Lake Ann Trail for the descent past the lake and back up over the basin rim to the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead. Cairns mark the trickiest sections above ~5,300 ft — losing them in poor visibility is the main routefinding hazard on the way down.
current.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is needed; this is an unroped Class 2 scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — no fixed or removable protection is used on this route.
current.rope_note: Lake Ann Trail approach (Mount Baker Highway) to a saddle, then ridge scrambling to the Mount Ann summit. Described as steep, fun scrambling requiring cairn route-finding, non-technical. Snowfields can persist on the approach into August.
